**On Looking**

This morning I stood at a window and watched a heron stand in a creek, and I realized I had been looking at the water for several minutes before I saw the bird at all. It was gray against gray, still as a fence post, folded into the reeds the way a word folds into a sentence. Once I saw it, I could not unsee it. The creek rearranged itself around this new fact. And I thought: how much of the world am I standing inside of right now, not seeing? How much of it is heron-shaped, waiting?

I want to write about attention. Not the kind that gets debated in op-eds — the attention economy, the stolen focus, the phones — though those debates are real enough, and I will get to them. I mean something older and stranger: attention as a way of being in the world, a discipline, a form of devotion even. What happens to a life when someone decides to actually see what is in front of them?

Consider first how badly most of us look. There is a famous experiment from cognitive psychology — the one where viewers watch people passing a basketball and half of them fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit strolling through the frame. The finding gets cited so often it has become a cliché, but the reason it stays famous is that everyone who watches the video recognizes themselves. We have all missed gorillas. We miss them daily. We walk the same street for years and could not say what color the doors are. We sit across from people at dinner, nodding, composing our next remark, and afterward cannot recall what they wore, whether they seemed tired, whether there was a scar on their left hand.

It isn't stupidity. The brain is doing exactly what it evolved to do: filtering ruthlessly, spending its limited resources on what seems urgent. A creature that stopped to catalog every leaf would be eaten before it finished the first branch. Attention is expensive. Evolution built us to skim. But what served us on the savanna imprisons us in the living room. Skimming was meant to be a strategy, not a habitat. Somewhere along the way, the exception became the rule, and we began to live our entire lives in the mode designed only for scanning for threats — which, notably, is also the mode of anxiety. To skim the world perpetually is to be perpetually braced. No wonder we're tired.

Watch a child in a garden and you see the alternative. A four-year-old does not walk through a garden; she orbits it. She stops because a worm has surfaced. She crouches. She waits. The worm does nothing interesting by adult standards — it writhes vaguely, retreats — and yet she gives it a full minute, two minutes, an eternity by the clock of childhood, where afternoons used to stretch like taffy. Then she looks up and notices a plane's contrail dissolving, and gives that her whole face too. Nothing is skimming. Everything is read closely.

We explain this as naivety — she hasn't learned what matters yet. But flip it over: maybe she simply hasn't yet been taught the great lie of adulthood, which is that most things don't matter. The child pays attention because attention costs her nothing; no inner accountant stands over her calculating returns. Adults pay attention only when compelled — by novelty, by threat, by desire — and so the world contracts down to a narrow band of the stimulating and the scary. The rest blurs into scenery. The tragedy is that the blurred part includes nearly everything worth having.

There is an old exercise in drawing instruction that demonstrates this better than any argument. Students are told to draw a hand — often their own, resting on the table — and the results come out cartoonish, fingers like sausages, proportions invented rather than observed. Then the instructor says something simple: draw it again, but this time spend ninety percent of your time looking and only ten percent drawing. Do not let the pencil move unless your eyes are on the hand. The second drawings transform. Not because skill arrived in the interval, but because the students finally *looked*. They discovered that a hand is not the thing they thought it was. Knuckles swell asymmetrically. Fingers taper in ways the mind never registered. The thumbnail sits at an angle. The mind's generic label — *hand* — had been standing in for the actual object for decades, the way a stock photo stands in for a city.

This is the secret shame of perception: most of what we "see" is memory. We glance, match the input to a stored category, and move on. Cat, tree, car, face. The categories were assembled long ago, in childhood, crudely, and we've been running on them ever since. Real attention is the act of overriding the category — of letting the particular thing in front of you resist what you already know about it. Every serious painter, every good writer, every decent scientist is doing versions of the same trick: refusing the label long enough to let the world surprise them. The physicist Richard Feynman liked to say that when he looked at a glass of wine he saw physics, biology, history, geometry — the whole universe in a glass. He wasn't being poetic. He was describing what happens when you decline to stop at the word *wine*.

Grief teaches this too, brutally. Anyone who has lost someone knows the phenomenon: afterward, the details sharpen. You remember, obsessively, things you never knew you noticed — the specific worn spot on the heel of his shoe, the way she held a pen too tight, the exact pitch of a laugh. In the raw weeks after a death, the whole sensory world can feel hyperreal, every object saturated with significance, because the mind is searching its records for traces of the person and finding them everywhere. Grief rips open the filter. It proves, horribly, that the capacity for total attention was in us all along — we simply needed catastrophe to unlock it. The question that haunted me after my own losses was why it takes catastrophe. Why do we wait until someone is gone to finally study them?

Maybe because attention feels free, and therefore worthless. It costs nothing to look at someone tomorrow. Except it costs everything, and the bill always arrives. Attention is the only currency that cannot be saved, only spent, and it spends continuously whether we direct it or not. Every hour, the attention goes somewhere — into a screen, into worry loops, into the middle distance. The question is never whether to pay attention but to whom, or to what. Unattended, it defaults to whatever is loudest. Attended, it becomes a choice, and choices accumulate into a life. Show me where your attention goes on an ordinary Tuesday, and I will tell you what you love — or at least what you currently serve in love's place.

Birdwatchers understand this better than almost anyone. To become even a casual birder is to submit to a curriculum in noticing. At first the trees are just noise — chirping static. But then someone points out the chickadee's two-note whistle, and suddenly you hear chickadees everywhere, in yards you've walked past for a decade. Then the nuthatch's nasal honk. Then the woodpecker's drumroll versus the flicker's. Within a season, the neighborhood soundscape has been rewritten from noise into voices. Nothing in the environment changed. The bandwidth did. This is the quiet miracle of trained attention: it doesn't add anything to the world; it removes blindness. The world was already this rich. You were already this poor.

And here is what the phone-era debates usually miss: the problem isn't merely that devices steal time. It's that they train the opposite muscle. Every swipe rehearses abandonment. Every feed teaches the eye to flee anything that doesn't reward within a second. After enough rehearsal, the deep-attention circuits go fallow — not destroyed, but rusted, slow to engage. Then a person sits in front of a mountain, or a child, or a page, and finds themselves unable to stay. They blame themselves for boredom, when really they've simply been drilled out of the skill. Attention is athletic. It responds to training and detraining exactly like a muscle does. Which means the situation is hopeful, because muscles rebuild.

Boredom, in fact, turns out to be the doorway. The first minutes of undistracted attention are almost always unpleasant — the itch, the reach for the pocket, the sense that surely something more important awaits. Push through and something peculiar happens: the boring thing starts generating interest. Watch rain on a window past the point of boredom and patterns emerge, rhythms, tiny dramas of droplets merging. Stare at a painting for twenty minutes — an eternity by museum standards, where the average artwork gets seconds — and it begins to move, to change, to answer questions you hadn't asked. The interest was never in the objects. It was waiting behind the threshold of patience. Boredom is the tollbooth; most people turn back at the tollbooth and conclude the road led nowhere.

None of this means attention is always sweet. Honest writing about attention has to admit that looking closely hurts sometimes. The person who truly attends to their marriage will see the problems the distracted one can coast past. The citizen who reads the news slowly, thoroughly, feels the weight the scroller dodges. Attention strips anesthesia. There's a reason we drink, scroll, and busy ourselves — anesthesia works, sort of. But the cost structure is cruel: numbness dulls pain and joy in equal measure, while attention intensifies both. You cannot choose the intensified joy without buying the intensified pain. People who seem most alive tend to be people who accepted that trade, whether consciously or not. Their sorrow is realer and so is their delight. The flat ones chose neither, or drifted into choosing neither, which amounts to the same thing.

The philosopher Simone Weil once wrote — paraphrasing loosely — that attention, taken to its highest degree, is the same thing as generosity. I've carried that idea for years, testing it against experience, and it keeps holding. Think about what it means to attend fully to another person: you set yourself aside. Your rehearsed responses, your cleverness, your hunger to be interesting — all suspended. For the duration of true listening, the other person occupies the foreground and you recede. This is the rarest gift there is, and everyone knows it instantly upon receiving it, the way you know warmth. Most conversations are two monologues negotiating for airspace. Occasionally, rarely, someone actually listens — leans their whole self toward you — and the conversation changes temperature. Nothing was given but attention. Everything was given.

So maybe the practice is simpler than the literature suggests. Not apps, not regimens, not digital sabbaths, though those have their place. Just this: pick something each day and refuse the label. The soup is never just soup — smell it like the first human ever to encounter onions. The person at the bus stop is never just a stranger — notice the book in her bag, the way she checks the sky. Your own street deserves one honest walk, unhurried, at dusk, when the light does its best work. Look at things longer than comfort recommends. Comfort is the enemy here; comfort is the category-label clicking into place, the mind saying *known, known, known* and closing the file.

The heron eventually moved. It unfolded — that impossible unfolding, neck extending like a telescope, the whole bird becoming twice its seated size — took two slow steps through the shallows, and stabbed at the water faster than sight. Came up empty. Stood again. Resumed its statue act, patient as geology. I watched for a long time, and the strange truth is that watching the heron watch the water felt like being taught something. Here was a creature that had made an entire existence out of attention. Stillness, patience, total presence, and then one perfect strike. It misses sometimes, I know. It stood back up empty-handed and simply resumed waiting, no drama, no self-recrimination visible in those yellow eyes.

I went inside and made coffee and the kitchen looked different — brighter-edged somehow, more itself. That's the residue of attention; it bleeds. Ten minutes of genuinely seeing one thing recalibrates the eyes for everything nearby. Which suggests the stakes aren't aesthetic, really, or not only. A person who practices seeing becomes harder to fool, slower to hate (hatred requires categories, not faces), quicker to wonder, and — this is the part I keep returning to — more likely to be present for the actual short span they've been given. The days pass regardless. The question the heron poses, motionless in the gray water, is whether we'll be here for any of them.

The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is an open-ended creative writing prompt. Let me think about what would make an interesting, substantive essay or piece of writing.

I could write about:
- A philosophical topic (time, memory, consciousness)
- A personal essay style piece
- Nature writing
- An exploration of some idea that fascinates me
- Something about language, books, cities, the sea

Let me write something genuine and thoughtful. I think I'll write about something like "the texture of ordinary time" or maybe about libraries, or about night, or about the concept of attention. Something with room for digression and beauty.

Let me try writing about attention — how we pay it, what it costs, what it means. Or perhaps about the sea. Or about ruins. Actually, let me do something a bit unexpected: an essay on the pleasure of being slightly lost — in cities, in books, in thought. That gives me room to wander structurally, which suits the prompt.

Or I could write about night shifts, or about the history of a single object like the pencil, or salt. Microhistory essays are lovely.

Let me go with an essay about attention and noticing — but framed through concrete scenes rather than abstraction. Maybe titled something like "On Looking Slowly." I'll weave together: walking, birds, the way children notice things, the way grief sharpens attention, cameras and phones, drawing as a discipline of seeing, and end with something about how attention might be a form of love.

I need roughly 2500 words. Let me aim for that. I'll write flowing prose, essayistic, with specific images. Let me draft carefully and keep count approximately — typically my paragraphs run 100-150 words each, so I'll need maybe 18-22 paragraphs.

Let me actually write it well. I want vivid specifics: herons, the sound of a refrigerator, drawing exercises, Betty Edwards, John Berger, Annie Dillard-ish moments without copying. I should avoid heavy quoting since I can't verify quotes precisely; I can allude to ideas generally without fabricating exact quotations.

Structure plan:
1. Opening scene: standing at a window watching a bird, realizing how little I usually see.
2. The speed of modern life and the economy of attention.
3. Children's attention — how they notice everything, why.
4. Learning to draw — the lesson that you must look longer than you think.
5. Grief and attention — how loss makes us look.
6. Attention in nature — birdwatchers, naturalists, the discipline of naming.
7. Cities and strangers — the flâneur, noticing people.
8. Boredom as a doorway to attention.
9. The counterargument — attention can be painful; sometimes distraction is mercy.
10. Attention as love — Simone Weil's idea (paraphrase, not exact quote).
11. Closing: return to the window/bird image, small resolution.

That's a solid arc. Now let me write with care, keeping sentences varied and concrete. Aim ~2500 words. I'll monitor length: I'll estimate as I go. Roughly 2500 words is long — let me be generous with development in each section.

Formatting: This should be flowing prose, an essay. Headers probably not needed — a title plus prose paragraphs feels right for a personal essay. Maybe use section breaks or just continuous paragraphs. Continuous paragraphs with a title seems most elegant. No lists. Long-form is exactly what was requested.
